questions.q: What is the main cost of a full sync approach, as described in this lesson?
options: Full sync cannot be scheduled on a fixed cadence
Full sync re-sends every record on every run regardless of whether it changed, which becomes expensive when only a small fraction of a large dataset actually changes day to day
Full sync is only compatible with the REST API, never the Bulk API
Full sync cannot be used for data migrations
questions.explain: Full sync's simplicity comes at a real cost: resending every record every run, even when only a tiny fraction changed, wastes processing capacity and runtime on both systems — a cost that grows directly with dataset size.

questions.q: What does delta (incremental) sync require that full sync does not?
options: A reliable way to know what changed since the last successful run, including correctly resuming after a partially failed run
A completely separate database from the source system
Delta sync requires nothing extra; it is strictly simpler than full sync in every respect
Delta sync can only be used with Change Data Capture and no other change-tracking mechanism
questions.explain: Delta sync's efficiency comes with a design cost: the process needs a reliable mechanism for identifying what changed since the last run, and needs to correctly handle a run that failed partway through rather than skipping or duplicating records.

questions.q: Why does this lesson instruct the reader to check Salesforce's current Bulk API limits page rather than memorize a specific figure from the lesson?
options: Because Bulk API limits are classified and cannot be published

Because the exact numeric limits (batch size, file size, rolling 24-hour record ceiling) vary across API versions and can change across releases, even though the underlying design intent of Bulk API stays the same
Because Bulk API has no documented limits at all
Because Salesforce removed Bulk API limits entirely in recent releases
questions.explain: Per Salesforce's own Bulk API limits documentation, the specific numeric allocations change across API versions and releases, so an architect should verify the current figures for the actual org and API version rather than relying on a number that may be outdated.

questions.q: A batch sync job fails at record 340,000 of 500,000. What does this lesson say the sync design must explicitly decide?
options: Nothing; every batch framework automatically handles partial failures identically

Whether the whole job fails atomically or partially applies and reports failed records, and how the next run reconciles that partially-applied state — a decision that depends on whether partial application is acceptable for that dataset
Whether to switch from Bulk API to the REST API permanently
Whether to abandon batch sync entirely in favor of real-time sync
questions.explain: Batch frameworks differ in how they handle partial failure — some fail atomically, others apply what they can — and the sync design has to explicitly choose and handle one behavior rather than discovering it by accident during an incident.

questions.q: What recurring failure mode does this lesson describe involving a batch job's scheduled time window?
options: A batch window sized with no headroom works fine until data volume grows, then starts running past its window and colliding with other scheduled work
Batch windows are never affected by data volume growth
Batch jobs cannot be scheduled to run overnight under any circumstances
Batch windows only matter for synchronous integrations, not batch sync
questions.explain: A batch job sized to just barely fit its window is fragile to growth — as volume increases, the job starts overrunning its window and colliding with the next scheduled job or the start of business hours, which is why headroom matters in batch-window planning.
